case_name: Shaurya Alloys and connected matters (batch of 424 writ petitions) v. Union of India & GST Authorities
citation: CWP-34296-2024 (O&M) and connected matters, Punjab & Haryana High Court, reserved 21 August 2026, pronounced 1 October 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Chief Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra and Justice Rohit Kapoor disposed of a batch of 424 writ petitions challenging denial or reversal of Input Tax Credit from purchasing dealers under Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act, where the selling dealer had defaulted on tax payment, filed nil/short returns, gone untraceable, or had its registration cancelled retrospectively. The Court upheld Section 16(2)(c) as constitutionally valid but held it cannot be applied mechanically or in isolation merely on proof of the supplier's default; read with Section 155 and provisions such as Sections 41, 73, 74, 75(12), 76 and 79 and Rules 36, 37A and 88C, officers must examine the genuineness of the transaction, actual receipt of goods/services, and the buyer's documentary evidence before denying credit. The Court laid down 14 detailed guidelines for proper officers across Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh covering notices, disclosure of relied-upon material, personal hearing, cross-examination and reasoned orders, and directed pending proceedings to be reconsidered accordingly with no fresh coercive recovery until fresh decisions are taken.
why_it_matters: Gives GST-registered buyers facing an ITC reversal notice over a supplier's default a detailed, enforceable procedural checklist to demand from the department, well beyond the bare principle that Section 16(2)(c) is valid — officers can no longer deny credit on a GSTR-2B mismatch alone.
